r1.text: Love that idea—let’s spin up a fresh space for it.

First up is “Warburg’s reading room,” a picture from the user’s own cards. It shows picture panels standing along the shelves of his library, which feels like a lovely cue for how ideas can hang and cluster in space.

There are 12 new cards in place, and I’d start with the “Virtual memory palaces: immersion aids recall” paper, because it speaks directly to how VR changes memory and brainstorming. If you want a next step, we can open that idea up and build a layer around it, like examples or design patterns to try in your own sessions.

n2.text: Nice angle—let’s build a fresh layer of related metaphors around that.

First up, there’s “A disc of pictures” by Eugene Pylinsky. It’s a circle crammed with hundreds of tiny images you see all at once, with no clear path through them. It feels like a big visual dump, not a journey.

That “Neurones poster” sounds like a great next stop—ideas as bursts feels nicely different from a palace or a mountain. After that, we could pull in one more metaphor that’s more about structure, like the grid or the ring, to balance the set.

mo.text: Nice, let’s expand that vibe and pull in some fresh angles around it.

A flower of nodes just landed, and it’s a lovely match. It’s one stalk that fans out into hundreds of colored dots, like a network drawn as a flower, which keeps that bursting energy but makes it feel organic.

There’s a whole constellation of options now, and I’d peek first at “A network grown from its centre” because those thousands of branching routes sound closest to the same bursting-but-structured feeling as the Neurones vibe. If you want, we can keep a couple of your favorites and build the next layer from those.

n3.text: Nice, let’s build a fresh layer around that organizing question.
First up, “Slice of Heartland.” It’s a film in your own cards, described as a tree drawn as 100 cross-sections, with one poster for each. It sounds like a really visual way to show structure.
Nine more came in, and my favorite is the “Linux file system” picture—one root with everything hanging from it is a clean mental model for keeping lots of pieces tidy.
One more arrived: “By time,” which shows each request as a new layer, with older ones fading back and the newest one lit.
Another one landed: “By branches,” where each question forks into its own path, growing alongside the others.

I’d start with “By depth,” because it keeps your focus on the newest layer while still showing the older context behind it, which feels perfect for a busy idea space. If you like that view, we can open it and use it as the default way to organize the ring.

f1.text: Nice thought—let’s spin that into a new layer on top of this.
First up, there’s “Underground map” by Harry Beck from 1934, shown as a picture. It’s from your own cards, and it’s a great example of simplifying a complex space so it’s easier to navigate.

I’d start with “Virtual reality on a WIM” because it’s a tidy idea: a whole-room model in your hand that helps you stay oriented and jump where you need to go. Next, we could keep that one and then pull in one or two contrasting navigation examples, like the stick chart or the Beck-style simplification, to compare approaches.

f2.text: Alright, let’s unpack that idea together and connect it to how this space works.

First up, there’s a paper called “Cone Trees” from 1991. It describes a tree of files in 3D, where each branch is a cone with the parent at the tip and its children arranged around the rim, and when you pick one, the tree turns to bring that path forward.
Four more showed up, and I’d start with “Tree of Science” because its branches map whole fields of knowledge to shared roots, which makes the structure feel very clear.
One more landed—“Kind or path?”—which neatly contrasts a branch as a category in a library with a branch as a question you pursued in a brainstorm.

I’d open “Kind or path?” first, because it nails the difference between structure as a category and structure as a growing line of inquiry, which is perfect for a brainstorming flow. If you want, we can keep going with one angle, like knowledge trees, evolution, or interface design, and build a deeper layer there.

f3.text: Okay, let’s spin up a new layer on that.

First up, there’s “Double Transparency” by Jesús Rafael Soto, from 1956. It’s described as two painted sheets layered so that, together, they create a third picture. It sounds like a lovely little illusion.
Six more came in, and my favorite is “Layer Drawings” by Nobuhiro Nakanishi—each clear sheet holds a moment, so the whole stack becomes a kind of time you can look through.
One more landed: “Layers blending,” where the older layers fold into a single plane, so a layer can melt into the next.

I’d start with “Layer Drawings” because it makes layering feel like time you can literally look through. If you want, I can help you pick one visual metaphor—like distance, time, or cuts—and build the next layer around that.

f4.text: Alright, let’s spin up some new angles to compare around this piece.

First up, there’s “Layers and Their Relationships,” one of your own notes. It’s a nice fit for comparing, because it’s already framed around how layers relate rather than just stacking them. I’d open it and see what distinctions you were drawing there.
Another one is “Layer study A2,” the version you chose on 12 November.
And there’s “Six looks for the minimap,” one journey drawn six ways side by side: rows, book, lotus, tree, territory, and metro.

I’d start with “Layers and Their Relationships,” because it’s your own framing and it should give the cleanest baseline for comparing the others. If you want, we can open that first and then pull out a simple comparison rubric from it.

px.text: Nice, let's spin up something you can actually try in the headset.
First up, there’s a picture called “Every film a dot round you.” It’s an earlier prototype: a few hundred films as dots on a single sphere, hanging in your room.
There’s one more: “Three films opened in one lasso,” where a line around a few dots makes a group, and each film opens in its own pane.
Another one is “Glass easels and a dial,” a workable room where a dial moves from the film in focus, through its stack, to everything.

I’d start with “Glass easels and a dial” because it sounds like the most usable right away: a clear control from one film to the whole set. Next, we could keep that one and then try a quick pass comparing it to the lasso grouping to see which feels more intuitive.

f5.text: Nice, that’s a rich rabbit hole—let me pull in some fresh angles around spatial memory.

Eight new cards landed, and I’d start with the 2017 paper on memory-palace training—it sounds like a clean bridge from the Data mountain idea to measurable changes in recall and brain networks. Next, want to focus on research first, or pull a design inspiration layer from the historical memory systems?

f7.text: There’s a picture called “Portraits standing on glass, MASP,” and visitors can actually walk behind the pictures. It’s a lovely way to make the display feel open and a bit surprising.

I’d start with “Casa de Vidro” because the idea of a glass house in the trees feels like a neat echo of those transparent easels. If you want to keep going, we can pull in a related angle, like how different spaces shape how people move through ideas.

f6.text: Let’s spin out a new layer from that thought and see who pops up.

The first one is a picture called “Abiding nowhere, the awakened mind arises” by Musō Soseki from the 14th century, and it’s from your own cards. It feels like a beautifully calm counterpoint to the idea of a big insight happening outdoors.

I’d open the Plato’s Academy mosaic first, because “philosophers gathered under a tree” is a perfect mirror to your theme of ideas in shared space. Want me to pull more like it, or help you keep a couple of these for your tree?

pi.text: Alright, let’s spin up a fresh layer around that idea.
A new card just landed: “Two hands set the zoom.” It shows that spreading your hands pulls things nearer, with a readout at 19 percent and a chain of beads below it.

I’d open “The go-go interaction technique” first, because it sounds like a practical way to reach distant objects without breaking the illusion. If you want, I can help you keep that one and then look for more interaction techniques to compare.

pd.text: Nice, let’s branch out from this example and pull in another historical reference.

I’d start with “Chironomia,” because mapping gestures into positions feels like a direct ancestor of today’s spatial interfaces. If you want, I can pull a bit more context around how that idea connects to modern VR thinking.

pg.text: Nice prompt—this is a good moment to choose what’s worth keeping.

First up, there’s a picture called “Figures for Chinese shadow puppets” by Juan Llorens from 1859, and it’s from your own cards. It’s a neat fit here because it’s literally about codified hand figures, which makes it a strong candidate for keeping as a reference point.
Two more landed: “A Sunset” by Caroline Furness Jayne from 1906, and “A Bird in Flight” by Henry Bursill from 1859.
Another one is “Our nine gestures,” which shows the app’s own set like pinch, hold, grab, mark, palms together, and flat hand.

I’d look at “Our nine gestures” first, because it’s the closest to how your app actually defines movement, so it gives you a clean baseline to compare everything else against. Next, you could keep that one and then pick one historical reference to pair with it for contrast.

fb.text: Nice, let’s spin up a new layer on that and gather some build-focused ideas.

I’d look at “Card program” first, because knowing the card types and arrangements gives you a structure to build around instead of improvising everything. After that, we can pull in “Hosting notes” to shape how sessions run and scale, or we can go find some concrete tool and workflow examples next.

bw.text: There’s a card showing an artwork called “Information desk,” from the Public Catalog Room at the New York Public Library, from 1926. It’s a neat historical reference for how information was organized in a grand, shared space.

I’d start with the “Information desk” card, because it gives a clear, grounded example of how a shared knowledge space was organized. If you want, we can add another layer looking at modern equivalents of that setup.

ba.text: A new card popped in: an artwork titled “Chinese Telephone Exchange,” from 1918. The note says a few people route every call, which is a neat fit for your “one voice over eight roles” idea.
I’d open “Who does what” first, because it spells out the one voice with eight roles idea in plain terms. Then a good next step is to keep that card and build the next layer from its wording.

bp.text: A new card just popped in: “Herbarium sheet.” It shows a pressed rose with its label on a single sheet, like a tidy little record of a plant.

I’d open “A catalogue of everything” first, because a card repertory feels like a perfect mirror for your FigJam board—organized ideas you can navigate. If you want, we can keep that one and then pull a new layer focused on how to structure or label clusters in your board.

bu.text: There’s a facts card called “The glass easels, in three dates,” from MASP. It’s about Lina Bo Bardi’s easels at MASP, which sounds like a lovely little design rabbit hole to peek into.
There’s also “Lina Bo Bardi,” noted as the architect of MASP and its glass easels.
And there’s “Rearrange by template,” showing your things laid out as a timeline, an A/B comparison, a matrix, or clusters.

I’d open “Rearrange by template” first, because it’s a quick, practical way to see how your ideas can snap into different shapes. If you like that direction, we can go deeper on one layout, like a timeline or a matrix, and build a layer around that.

bi.text: First up, there’s a paper called “Put-that-there” from 1980. It’s about a simple voice-and-gesture command: you say “put that there” while pointing at a wall-sized screen, and the system figures out what “that” and “there” mean from your hand and voice together.

I’d start with “Put-that-there,” because it nails the core idea of mixing voice and gesture into one clean command, which is very close to how your board describes features and interactions. Next, we could pull in a few more historical interface examples to compare, or you can pick one feature on your board and we’ll map how it might work in VR.

bv.text: Let me check what you’ve already saved under that name.
First up, there’s an artwork called “His Master’s Voice” by Francis Barraud from 1898. The card’s note is simple: Nipper listens.

I’d start with that “His Master’s Voice” card, because it looks like the only thing that surfaced and it might be a misfire for Bo Bardi. If you want, I can try again with a broader search, like “Lina Bo Bardi” or related projects.

bq.text: A new card just landed called “Questions Momo offers.” It’s a list of three or four prompts that appear under an open card, written in my voice.
I’d start with “Questions Momo offers” because it can shape how you explore the rest of the board. If you want, we can pull one more layer from it to test what those prompts actually spark.

bn.text: Let’s zoom in on what this bit suggests.
It’s a manicule, a little pointing hand a reader drew in the margin to highlight something. It’s basically an old-school “look here” marker.

I’d start with the manicule because it’s such a crisp metaphor for marking what matters—perfect for a FigJam workflow. If you’d like, we can build the next layer around how to use visual markers to guide a session.

bh.text: Nice, the first thing that showed is “What runs where.” It says the headset draws and listens, while the Mac thinks and remembers.

I’d open “What runs where” first, because it’s a clean backbone: who does the sensing and sketching, and who does the heavy thinking. Next, we can add a layer for failure modes, like what happens if the Mac drops out or the headset can’t hear well.

rz.text: A new card just popped in: “Full Moon” by N. W. Pease, mid-1800s, and it’s from your own cards. It’s a lovely match for “Celestial Globe,” like a quiet night-sky counterpart.

I’d open “A Philosopher Lecturing on the Orrery” first, because it ties the cosmic theme to people learning together, which is very memory-palace friendly. If you want to keep exploring, I’d say we add another layer focused on how people visualize the sky in different eras.

f15.text: Okay, let’s build on that and see what pops up.
First up is a card called “Mnemosyne,” an artwork by Dante Gabriel Rossetti. It frames memory as the mother of the nine Muses, which is a lovely way to name the source of inspiration.

Nice, that brought up a little cluster of memory imagery—let me wrap it together. I’d start with the memory palace angle, because it connects directly to how people structure ideas in space, which feels very headset-friendly. If you want, I can help you pull a thread from that into a quick comparison with the world-tree metaphor.

ry.text: The first one is “Hanging Colors,” and it’s from your own cards. It’s about architecture portfolio projects and tips for high school students. It’s a neat, practical angle to pair with that dreamy “ideas as vessels” vibe.

I’d start with “Coloured discs in a hotel” because it sounds like a ready-made mood and spatial vibe you could borrow for the headset scene. If you want, I can help you keep a couple of the strongest references and build the next layer from those.

r10.text: Interesting one—let’s talk about the word people usually use for that.

The first thing that landed is a picture called “Fireworks at Ryōgoku” by Utagawa Hiroshige from 1858, from your own cards. It’s a lovely surprise in this layer, even if it’s not the bird term you were asking about.

I’d open “Starlings at dusk” first because it sounds closest to that feeling of a flock shifting together in a single sweep. Want to keep that one and then we can look for a simple definition you can use in your notes?

rw.text: Okay, let’s pull in a new layer around that neuron and see what shows up.
First up, a picture called "Traveler on a Road in a Forest" by Maxime Lalanne from 1866, from your own cards. It’s a lovely contrast to the neuron—another kind of branching path, but in a landscape.

I’d open the “Net transfer of carbon…” paper first, because it mirrors the neuron’s logic: separate bodies, one network. If you want, we can go deeper into the shared-network angle, or pivot to the visual tree analogies.
